Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the space element.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of the space element;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the space element;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of the space element.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the consciousness-element;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of the consciousness-element;
nor, apart from the suchness of the consciousness-element, is he conjoined or disjoined.
It is not otherwise than the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the consciousness element that he is either conjoined or disjoined.
Kauśika, that which is the Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of ignorance,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of ignorance.
Apart from the suchness of ignorance, he is neither joined nor disjoined;
apart from the true nature of ignorance, he is neither joined nor disjoined.
Kauśika, that which is the Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined with the suchness of conditioned formations.
It is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of formations;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the nature of formations;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything apart from the nature of formations.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of consciousness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of consciousness;
and he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of consciousness.
Apart from the true nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dharmatā*), he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-tathatā*),
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-dharmatā*).
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of name-and-form;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of name-and-form.
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the six sense-bases.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of the six sense bases;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the suchness of the six sense bases;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the true nature of the six sense bases.
Kauśika,
that Tathāgata is neither joined to nor dissociated from the suchness of contact;
he is neither joined to nor dissociated from the dharmic nature of contact.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the suchness of contact;

he is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the dharmic nature of contact. Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of feeling, nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmic nature of feeling.
Apart from the suchness of feeling, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
apart from the dharma-nature of feeling, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of craving.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of craving;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of craving;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything apart from the dharmatā of craving.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of grasping;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharma-nature of grasping;
nor is he conjoined or disjoined with anything other than the suchness of grasping.
It is nowhere else than in the nature of appropriation that one is neither joined nor disjoined;
for, Kauśika, that which is the Tathāgata is not joined nor disjoined with the nature of becoming,
nor is he joined nor disjoined with the nature of existence.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of existence;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of existence.
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of birth.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the nature of birth;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of birth;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the nature of the dharma of birth.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the suchness of old age and death;
he is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the nature of old age and death;
nor is he conjoined with or disjoined from anything other than the suchness of old age and death.
Apart from the nature of aging and death, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined.
Kausika, that Tathagata is not conjoined with nor disjoined from the suchness of the perfection of giving;
he is not conjoined with nor disjoined from the dharmic nature of the perfection of giving.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the perfection of generosity;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the perfection of generosity.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the perfection of ethical discipline.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the perfection of ethical discipline;

he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of the perfection of ethical discipline; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything apart from the dharmatā of the perfection of ethical discipline.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the perfection of patience;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of the perfection of patience;
nor, indeed, is he conjoined or disjoined apart from the suchness of the perfection of patience.
Nor is he joined to, nor disjoined from, the true nature of the perfection of patience;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined to nor disjoined from the true nature of the perfection of vigor.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the perfection of vigor;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of the perfection of vigor;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the perfection of vigor.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined from the suchness of the perfection of meditation;
he is neither joined nor disjoined from the dharmatā of the perfection of meditation;
nor is he joined or disjoined apart from the suchness of the perfection of meditation.
Apart from the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the perfection of meditation, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the perfection of wisdom,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of the perfection of wisdom.

He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the perfection of wisdom; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature (dharmatā) of the perfection of wisdom.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of internal emptiness.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of internal emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of internal emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of internal emptiness.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of external emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of external emptiness;
nor is he conjoined or disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of external emptiness.
Apart from the dharmatā of external emptiness, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of internal-and-external emptiness,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of internal-and-external emptiness.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of internal-and-external emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature (*dharmatā*) of internal-and-external emptiness.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of emptiness.
He is neither joined nor disjoined from the reality-nature (dharmatā) of the emptiness of emptiness;
he is neither joined nor disjoined from anything other than the suchness (tathatā) of the emptiness of emptiness;
he is neither joined nor disjoined from anything other than the reality-nature of the emptiness of emptiness.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of great emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of great emptiness;
nor is he conjoined or disjoined with anything other than the suchness of great emptiness.
Apart from the dharmatā of great emptiness, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of ultimate emptiness,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of ultimate emptiness.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of ultimate emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of ultimate emptiness.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of the conditioned;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of the conditioned;
nor is he conjoined or disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of the emptiness of the conditioned.
Apart from the dharmic nature of the emptiness of the conditioned, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of the unconditioned,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmic nature of the emptiness of the unconditioned.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the emptiness of the unconditioned;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the emptiness of the unconditioned.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of absolute emptiness.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of absolute emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of absolute emptiness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of absolute emptiness.

Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharma-nature of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end; and he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the reality-nature (*dharmatā*) of beginningless and endless emptiness;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness (*tathatā*) of non-dispersal emptiness,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the reality-nature of non-dispersal emptiness.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the emptiness of non-dispersal;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of the emptiness of non-dispersal.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
He is neither joined nor disjoined from the dharmic nature of natural emptiness;
he is neither joined nor disjoined apart from the suchness of natural emptiness;
he is neither joined nor disjoined apart from the dharmic nature of natural emptiness.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of all dharmas;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of all dharmas;
nor is he conjoined or disjoined apart from the dharma-nature of the emptiness of all dharmas.
Apart from the dharmatā of the emptiness of all phenomena, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of own-characteristics,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of the emptiness of own-characteristics.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the emptiness of own-characteristics;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharma-nature of the emptiness of own-characteristics;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of non-apprehension.
He is neither joined nor disjoined with the true nature of non-apprehension and emptiness;
he is neither joined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of non-apprehension and emptiness.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of the emptiness of non-apprehension;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of non-existence,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of the emptiness of non-existence.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the emptiness of non-existence;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of the emptiness of non-existence.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmic nature of the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the suchness of the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the dharmic nature of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharma-nature of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
and he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the applications of mindfulness,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of the applications of mindfulness.
Apart from the suchness of the applications of mindfulness, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
apart from the true nature of the applications of mindfulness, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined.
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the right efforts.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the right efforts;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of the right efforts;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the right efforts.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the bases of psychic power;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmic nature of the bases of psychic power;
nor is he conjoined or disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the bases of psychic power.
Apart from the true nature of the bases of psychic power, he is neither joined nor disjoined; Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined with the suchness of the faculties,
and he is neither joined nor disjoined with the true nature of the faculties.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the sense faculties;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the sense faculties. Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the powers.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the nature of the powers;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the powers;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the nature of the powers.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined from the suchness of the factors of enlightenment;
he is neither joined nor disjoined from the true nature of the factors of enlightenment;
nor is he joined or disjoined elsewhere than from the suchness of the factors of enlightenment.
Apart from the true nature of the factors of enlightenment, he is neither joined nor disjoined;
Kausika, that Tathagata is neither joined nor disjoined with the suchness of the noble eightfold path,
nor is he joined nor disjoined with the true nature of the noble eightfold path.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the noble eightfold path;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the noble eightfold path.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the noble truths.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the noble truths;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of the noble truths;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the noble truths.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined from the suchness of meditative concentration;
he is neither joined nor disjoined from the dharmic nature of meditative concentration;
nor is he joined or disjoined elsewhere than from the suchness of meditative concentration.
Apart from the nature of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-dharmatā*), he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the reality of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa-tathatā*),
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the nature of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa-dharmatā*).

He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the immeasurables; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharma-nature of the immeasurables.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the formless attainments.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the formless attainments;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of the formless attainments;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the formless attainments.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined to nor disjoined from the suchness of liberation;
he is neither joined to nor disjoined from the true nature of liberation;
nor is he joined to or disjoined from anything other than the suchness of liberation.
Apart from the nature of liberation, he is neither joined nor disjoined;
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined with the suchness of the successive meditative attainments,
nor is he joined nor disjoined with the nature of the successive meditative attainments.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling.
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined from the suchness of the supernormal knowledges; he is neither joined nor disjoined from the true nature of the supernormal knowledges; nor is he joined or disjoined apart from the suchness of the supernormal knowledges.
Apart from the nature of the superknowledges,
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of meditative concentration.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of concentration;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of concentration;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of concentration.

Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined to nor disjoined from the suchness of the gateways of mnemonic formulas; he is neither joined to nor disjoined from the true nature of the gateways of mnemonic formulas; nor is he joined to or disjoined from anything other than the suchness of the gateways of mnemonic formulas.
Apart from the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the gateways of dhāraṇī, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
O Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness (*tathatā*) of the powers of a Tathāgata,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of the powers of a Tathāgata.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined from the suchness of the powers of a Tathāgata;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined from the dharmatā of the powers of a Tathāgata.
Kauśika, that which is a Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined from the suchness of the fearlessnesses.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the nature of fearlessness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of fearlessness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the nature of fearlessness.

Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the analytical knowledges; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of the analytical knowledges; nor is he conjoined or disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the analytical knowledges.
Apart from the dharmatā of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), he is neither joined nor disjoined;
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined with the suchness (tathatā) of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling (anupūrvavihārasamāpatti),
nor is he joined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

He is neither joined nor disjoined with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he is neither joined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he is neither joined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined from the suchness of the superknowledges; he is neither joined nor disjoined from the true nature of the superknowledges; he is neither joined nor disjoined from anything other than the suchness of the superknowledges.
Apart from the true nature of the superknowledges, he is neither joined nor disjoined;
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined with the suchness of meditative concentration,
nor is he joined nor disjoined with the true nature of meditative concentration.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of concentration;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of concentration.

Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the suchness of the gateways of dhāraṇī; he is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the true nature of the gateways of dhāraṇī; nor is he conjoined with or disjoined from anything other than the suchness of the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Apart from the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
for that Tathāgata, Kauśika, is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness (*tathatā*) of the powers of a Tathāgata,
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the true nature of the powers of a Tathāgata.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the Tathāgata’s powers;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the Tathāgata’s powers.
Kauśika, that which is the Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the fearlessnesses.
He is neither joined nor disjoined from the nature of fearlessness;
he is neither joined nor disjoined from anything other than the suchness of fearlessness;
he is neither joined nor disjoined from anything other than the dharma-nature of fearlessness.

Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined from the suchness of the analytical knowledges; he is neither joined nor disjoined from the dharmatā of the analytical knowledges; nor is he joined or disjoined in any way other than from the suchness of the analytical knowledges.
Apart from the dharma-nature of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), he is neither joined nor disjoined;
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined with the suchness of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī-tathatā*),
nor is he joined nor disjoined with the dharma-nature of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī-dharmatā*).
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of great loving-kindness;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of great loving-kindness.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of great compassion.
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the dharmatā of great compassion;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of great compassion;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of great compassion.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither joined nor disjoined from the suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha;

he is neither joined nor disjoined from the true nature of the unique qualities of a Buddha; he is neither joined nor disjoined from anything other than the suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Except for the nature of the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), he is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of omniscience (*sarvajñatātathatā*),
nor is he conjoined nor disjoined with the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatādharmatā*).
He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of omniscience;
he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the dharmatā of omniscience.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
He is neither joined to nor disjoined from the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
he is neither joined to nor disjoined from anything other than the suchness (*tathatā*) of the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
he is neither joined to nor disjoined from anything other than the true nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
Kauśika, that Tathāgata is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the suchness of all-aspect omniscience;
he is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the dharmatā of all-aspect omniscience.

He is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined with anything other than the true nature of the knowledge of all aspects. Kauśika, the Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined with all these dharmas.
This is its power; this is its empowerment, by way of non-empowerment.
Furthermore, Kauśika, as to what you asked:
"From where should a bodhisattva mahāsattva seek the perfection of wisdom?"
Kauśika, it is not to be sought in form, nor is it to be sought apart from form; it is not to be sought in feeling, nor is it to be sought apart from feeling;
it is not to be sought in perception, nor is it to be sought apart from perception.
It is not to be sought within the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nor is it to be sought apart from the formative forces;
it is not to be sought within consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor is it to be sought apart from consciousness. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, whatever is form, whatever is feeling, whatever is perception, whatever are the formative forces, and whatever is consciousness—

The Bodhisattva, and the perfection of wisdom, and the great compassion, and the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the eye, nor should he seek it apart from the eye.
It is not to be sought in the ear, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the ear;
it is not to be sought in the nose, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the nose;
it is not to be sought in the tongue, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the tongue.
It is not to be sought in the body, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the body;
it is not to be sought in the mind, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the mind. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, that which is the eye, that which is the ear, that which is the nose, that which is the tongue, that which is the body, that which is the mind, that which is the bodhisattva, and that which is the perfection of wisdom—[all these are of one suchness].

and their investigation—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in form, nor should he seek it apart from form.
It is not to be sought from sound, nor is it to be sought apart from sound; it is not to be sought from odor, nor is it to be sought apart from odor;
it is not to be sought from taste, nor is it to be sought apart from taste.
It is not to be sought in contact, nor is it to be sought apart from contact;
it is not to be sought in phenomena, nor is it to be sought apart from phenomena. For what reason?

For it is thus, Kauśika: whatever form, whatever sound, whatever odor, whatever taste, whatever tangible object, whatever phenomena, whatever bodhisattva, whatever perfection of wisdom, and whatever seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in visual consciousness, nor should he seek it apart from visual consciousness;

he should not seek it in auditory consciousness, nor should he seek it apart from auditory consciousness; he should not seek it in olfactory consciousness, nor should he seek it apart from olfactory consciousness.
It is not to be sought from tongue-consciousness, nor is it to be sought apart from tongue-consciousness;
it is not to be sought from body-consciousness, nor is it to be sought apart from body-consciousness;
it is not to be sought from mind-consciousness, nor is it to be sought apart from mind-consciousness. Why is that?

For in this way, Kauśika: that which is eye-consciousness, that which is ear-consciousness, that which is nose-consciousness, that which is tongue-consciousness, that which is body-consciousness, that which is mind-consciousness; and that which is the bodhisattva, and that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—[all these are non-dual].
All these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-resistant, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom through visual contact, nor should he seek it apart from visual contact;
he should not seek it through auditory contact, nor should he seek it apart from auditory contact.
It is not to be sought in olfactory contact, nor is it to be sought apart from olfactory contact; it is not to be sought in gustatory contact, nor is it to be sought apart from gustatory contact;
it is not to be sought in tactile contact, nor is it to be sought apart from tactile contact.
It is not to be sought from mental contact, nor is it to be sought apart from mental contact. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, whatever is visual contact, whatever is auditory contact, whatever is olfactory contact, whatever is gustatory contact, whatever is tactile contact, whatever is mental contact, and whatever is a bodhisattva—[all these are non-dual].

Both that which is the perfection of wisdom and that which is the seeking—these dharmas are all neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the feeling conditioned by eye-contact, nor elsewhere than in the feeling conditioned by eye-contact.
It is not to be sought in the sensation conditioned by ear-contact, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the sensation conditioned by ear-contact;
it is not to be sought in the sensation conditioned by nose-contact, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the sensation conditioned by nose-contact.

It is not to be sought in the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact; it is not to be sought in the feeling conditioned by body-contact, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the feeling conditioned by body-contact; it is not to be sought in the feeling conditioned by mind-contact, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the feeling conditioned by mind-contact. Why is that?

For in this way, Kauśika, that which is feeling conditioned by eye-contact, that which is feeling conditioned by ear-contact, that which is feeling conditioned by nose-contact, that which is feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, that which is feeling conditioned by body-contact,
that which is feeling conditioned by mind-contact; and the bodhisattva, and the perfection of wisdom, and the seeking— [all these are non-dual].

All these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the earth element, nor should it be sought elsewhere than in the earth element; it should not be sought in the water element, nor should it be sought elsewhere than in the water element.
It is not to be sought in the fire element, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the fire element;
it is not to be sought in the wind element, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the wind element;
it is not to be sought in the space element, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the space element.
It is not to be sought within the element of consciousness, nor is it to be sought apart from the element of consciousness. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element, the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom, and the search itself—[all these are not two, nor are they distinct].

All these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in ignorance, nor should he seek it apart from ignorance;
he should not seek it in volitional formations, nor should he seek it apart from volitional formations.
It is not to be sought apart from consciousness, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than consciousness;
it is not to be sought apart from name-and-form, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than name-and-form;
it is not to be sought apart from the six sense bases, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than the six sense bases.
It is not to be sought in contact, nor is it to be sought apart from contact; it is not to be sought in feeling, nor is it to be sought apart from feeling;
it is not to be sought in craving, nor is it to be sought apart from craving.
It is not to be sought in grasping, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in grasping;
it is not to be sought in becoming, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in becoming;
it is not to be sought in birth, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in birth.
It is not to be sought apart from old age and death, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than from old age and death. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, that which is ignorance, those which are formations, that which is consciousness, that which is name-and-form, that which is the six sense-bases, that which is contact, that which is feeling, that which is craving, that which is grasping, that which is becoming, that which is birth, that which is old age and death, as well as the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom, and that which is... [the rest of the sentence continues].
All these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being characterless.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the perfection of giving, nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the perfection of giving;
he should not seek it apart from the perfection of ethical discipline, nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the perfection of ethical discipline.
It is not to be sought apart from the perfection of patience, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than the perfection of patience;
it is not to be sought apart from the perfection of vigor, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than the perfection of vigor;
it is not to be sought apart from the perfection of meditation, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than the perfection of meditation.
The perfection of wisdom is not to be sought apart from the perfection of wisdom, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, that which is the perfection of giving, that which is the perfection of ethical discipline, that which is the perfection of patience, that which is the perfection of vigor, that which is the perfection of meditative concentration, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the bodhisattva—[all these are not different].

The perfection of wisdom and the search for it—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in internal emptiness, nor should he seek it apart from internal emptiness.
It is not to be sought outside of external emptiness, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than external emptiness;
it is not to be sought outside of internal-external emptiness, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than internal-external emptiness;
it is not to be sought outside of the emptiness of emptiness, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than the emptiness of emptiness.

It is not to be sought within great emptiness, nor is it to be sought apart from great emptiness; it is not to be sought within ultimate emptiness, nor is it to be sought apart from ultimate emptiness;
it is not to be sought within conditioned emptiness, nor is it to be sought apart from conditioned emptiness.
It is not to be sought apart from the emptiness of the unconditioned, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the emptiness of the unconditioned;
it is not to be sought apart from absolute emptiness, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in absolute emptiness;
it is not to be sought apart from the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end.
It is not to be sought apart from the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the emptiness of non-dispersal;
it is not to be sought apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
it is not to be sought apart from the emptiness of all phenomena, nor is it to be sought elsewhere than in the emptiness of all phenomena.
It is not to be sought in the emptiness of specific characteristics, nor elsewhere than in the emptiness of specific characteristics;

it is not to be sought in the emptiness of non-apprehension, nor elsewhere than in the emptiness of non-apprehension; it is not to be sought in the emptiness of non-existence, nor elsewhere than in the emptiness of non-existence. (ŚsP_II-3_150)
It should be sought within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, but not sought elsewhere than within the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
it should not be sought within the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, nor sought elsewhere than within the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, that which is internal emptiness, that which is external emptiness, and that which is internal-external emptiness—[are all one].
The emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned,

the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, and the emptiness of non-apprehension.

The emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom, and the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) apart from the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), nor should he seek it elsewhere than within the applications of mindfulness. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, those which are the applications of mindfulness, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these [are non-dual].
All these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the right efforts, nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the right efforts.
Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: the right efforts, the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom, and the search—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should seek the perfection of wisdom not apart from the bases of psychic power, nor elsewhere than in the bases of psychic power. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the faculties (*indriya*), nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the faculties. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: those sense-faculties, that Bodhisattva, that perfection of wisdom, and that seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the perfection of wisdom...
They are not to be sought apart from the powers, nor are they to be sought elsewhere than in the powers. For what reason?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the powers, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) apart from the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the factors of enlightenment. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the factors of enlightenment, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the noble eightfold path, nor should he seek it other than within the noble eightfold path. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, the noble eightfold path, the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom, and the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-resistant, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the noble truths, nor should he seek it other than within the noble truths. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the noble truths, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the meditative concentrations, nor should he seek it apart from the meditative concentrations. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the meditative concentrations, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the immeasurables, nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the immeasurables. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the immeasurables, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), nor should he seek it apart from the formless attainments. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the formless attainments, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in the liberations (vimokṣa), nor should he seek it in the liberations. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the liberations, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, non-demonstrable, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) apart from the successive attainments of meditative dwelling (anupūrvavihārasamāpatti), nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the successive attainments of meditative dwelling. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, those successive attainments of meditative dwelling, that bodhisattva, that perfection of wisdom, and that seeking—[all these are non-dual].

All these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: those gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the Bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom, and the seeking—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the superknowledges (abhijñā), nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the superknowledges. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the seeking—all these phenomena (*dharma*) are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom within the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), nor should he seek it apart from the meditative concentrations. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: whatever concentrations there are, whatever bodhisattva there is, whatever perfection of wisdom there is, and whatever seeking there is—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom from the gateways of mnemonic formulas (dhāraṇī), nor should he seek it elsewhere than from the gateways of mnemonic formulas. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom, and the seeking—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the powers of a Tathāgata, nor should he seek it other than within the powers of a Tathāgata. That...
For what reason?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the powers of a Tathāgata, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) apart from the grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya), nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the grounds of self-confidence. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those grounds of self-confidence, that bodhisattva, that perfection of wisdom, and that seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom from the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), nor should he seek it from the analytical knowledges. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those analytical knowledges, that bodhisattva, that perfection of wisdom, and that seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from great loving-kindness, nor should he seek it elsewhere than in great loving-kindness. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, that which is great loving-kindness, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from great compassion, nor should he seek it elsewhere than within great compassion. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, that which is great compassion, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), nor should he seek it elsewhere than within the unique qualities of a buddha.
Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, those which are the unique qualities of a buddha, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these are one and the same.

All these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from omniscience, nor should it be sought elsewhere than in omniscience. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, that which is omniscience, that which is the bodhisattva, and [that which is the perfection of wisdom]—[all these are not two, nor are they distinct].

The perfection of wisdom and that which is the seeking [of it]—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom in the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor should he seek it apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), the bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the seeking—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not seek the perfection of wisdom apart from the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor should he seek it elsewhere than in the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: that which is the knowledge of all aspects, that which is the bodhisattva, that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the seeking—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Why is that?
For thus it is: form is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom other than form;
the suchness of form is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom other than the suchness of form;
the dharmatā of form is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom other than the dharmatā of form.
Perfection of wisdom is not sensation, nor is perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in sensation;
perfection of wisdom is not the suchness of sensation, nor is perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in the suchness of sensation;
perfection of wisdom is not the true nature of sensation, nor is perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in the true nature of sensation.
The perfection of wisdom is not perception, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in perception;
the perfection of wisdom is not the suchness of perception, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in the suchness of perception;
the perfection of wisdom is not the true nature of perception, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in the true nature of perception.
The perfection of wisdom is not the formative forces, nor is the perfection of wisdom apart from the formative forces;

the perfection of wisdom is not the suchness of the formative forces, nor is the perfection of wisdom apart from the suchness of the formative forces; the perfection of wisdom is not the true nature of the formative forces, nor is the perfection of wisdom apart from the true nature of the formative forces.
The perfection of wisdom is not consciousness, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in consciousness;
the perfection of wisdom is not the suchness of consciousness, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in the suchness of consciousness;
the perfection of wisdom is not the true nature of consciousness, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in the true nature of consciousness.
The eye is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the eye;
the suchness of the eye is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the suchness of the eye;
the nature of phenomena of the eye is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the nature of phenomena of the eye.
The ear is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the ear;
the suchness of the ear is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the suchness of the ear;
the true nature of the ear is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the true nature of the ear.
The nose is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the nose;
the suchness of the nose is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the suchness of the nose;
the nature of phenomena of the nose is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the nature of phenomena of the nose.
The tongue is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the tongue;
the suchness of the tongue is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the suchness of the tongue;
the true nature of the tongue is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the true nature of the tongue.
The body is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom apart from the body;
the suchness of the body is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom apart from the suchness of the body;
the nature of the body is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom apart from the nature of the body.
The perfection of wisdom is not the mind, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the mind;
the perfection of wisdom is not the suchness of the mind, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than the suchness of the mind;

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the elder Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas;
venerable Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the immeasurable perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; venerable [Subhūti], this perfection of wisdom is the infinite perfection."
Subhūti, it is this very perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas,
in which those training have attained, are attaining, and will attain the fruit of stream-entry.

By those who are once-returners, the fruit of once-returning has been attained, is being attained, and will be attained; by those who are non-returners, the fruit of non-returning has been attained, is being attained, and will be attained;

and training therein, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having matured sentient beings and purified a buddha-field, have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

because it has reached the state of ultimate emptiness, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
For in this way, Kauśika, in absolute emptiness no beginning is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Because it has reached the greatness of emptiness that is without end or beginning, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, in the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end, no prior limit is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Because of its vastness, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, by virtue of the emptiness of non-dispersal. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, in the emptiness of non-apprehension, no prior limit is perceived, no subsequent limit is perceived, and no middle is perceived;
because of its vastness as the emptiness of intrinsic nature, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, no prior limit of essential emptiness is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Because of the vastness of the emptiness of all phenomena, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, in the emptiness of all dharmas, no prior limit is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Because it has reached the greatness of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, within the emptiness of specific characteristics, no prior limit is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended,
and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because it has reached the greatness of the emptiness of non-apprehension, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, in the emptiness of non-apprehension, no prior limit is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because it has reached the greatness of the emptiness of non-existence, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, in the emptiness of non-existence, no prior limit is perceived, no subsequent limit is perceived, and no middle is perceived.
Kauśika, because it has reached the greatness of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no prior limit is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because it has reached the greatness of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, no prior limit is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because of the greatness of the foundations of mindfulness, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no beginning of the foundations of mindfulness is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because of the greatness of the right efforts, this is a great perfection for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, no beginning of the right efforts is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because of the greatness of the bases of psychic power, this is a great perfection for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, no beginning of the bases of psychic power is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because their faculties are so vast, this is a great perfection for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no beginning of the faculties is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because it has reached the greatness of power, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, of these powers, no prior limit is perceived, no subsequent limit is perceived, and no middle is perceived.
Kauśika, because the factors of enlightenment are vast, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no beginning of the factors of enlightenment is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because it has reached the greatness of the noble eightfold path, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no beginning of the noble eightfold path is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Kauśika, because it has reached the greatness of the noble truths, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of the noble truths is apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle can be apprehended;
Kauśika, because of the greatness of the meditations, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of the meditations can be apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle is apprehended;
because it is immeasurable and vast, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, for things that are immeasurable, no prior limit is apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle can be apprehended;
because of the greatness of the formless attainments, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of the formless attainments can be apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle is apprehended;
because of the vastness of the liberations, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of the liberations is apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle can be apprehended;
Kauśika, because of the greatness of the attainments of the successive dwellings, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, in the case of the attainments of the successive dwellings, no prior limit can be apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle is apprehended;
because of the vastness of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, for the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—no prior limit is apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle can be apprehended;
Kauśika, because the higher knowledges have reached greatness, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of the higher knowledges can be apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle is perceived;
because of the vastness of their concentration, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of concentrations is perceived.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle is apprehended;
Kauśika, because of the vastness of the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, this is a great perfection for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of the gateways of the dhāraṇīs is apprehended.
Neither a subsequent limit nor a middle is apprehended;
because of the greatness of the powers of a Tathāgata, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no prior limit of the powers of a Tathāgata is apprehended.
Neither the future limit nor the middle is apprehended;
because it has reached the greatness of fearlessness, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, [it is thus].
The limits of the grounds of self-confidence are not apprehended in the past, nor are they apprehended in the future, nor are they apprehended in the middle;
because of their having reached greatness through the analytical knowledges, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
For in this way, Kauśika, no beginning of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended;
because of its great extensiveness, Kauśika, this is the great perfection (mahāpāramitā) of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For it is thus, Kauśika: the great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) is not apprehended at the prior limit, nor is it apprehended at the subsequent limit, nor is it apprehended in the middle.
Because of its vastness, Kauśika, this is the great perfection (*mahāpāramitā*) of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
For in this way, Kauśika, no beginning of great compassion is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended;
because it has reached the greatness of the unique qualities of a Buddha, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, no prior limit of the unique qualities of a Buddha is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
Because they have reached the greatness of omniscience, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, no prior limit of omniscience is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended;
because it has reached the greatness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, the knowledge of the aspects of the path is not apprehended at its prior limit, nor is it apprehended at its subsequent limit, nor is it apprehended in the middle;
because it has reached the greatness of the knowledge of all aspects, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas. Why is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, no beginning of omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended.
By this method, Kauśika, this is the great perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, namely, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Because form is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection is immeasurable for bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no measure of form is apprehended; just as, Kauśika, no measure of space is apprehended.
In the same way, Kauśika, no measure of form is apprehended;
because space is immeasurable, form is immeasurable, and because form is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Because feeling is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is immeasurable. For what reason?
For in this way, Kauśika, no measure of feeling is apprehended; just as, Kauśika, no measure of space is apprehended,
even so, Kauśika, no measure of feeling is apprehended.
Because space is immeasurable, feeling is immeasurable;
because feeling is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Because perception is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is immeasurable. For what reason is that?
For in this way, Kauśika, no measure of perception (saṃjñā) is apprehended;
just as, Kauśika, no measure of space is apprehended,
even so, Kauśika, no measure of perception is apprehended.
Because space is immeasurable, perception is immeasurable; because perception is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is immeasurable. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no measure of conditioned phenomena is apprehended.
Just as, Kauśika, the measure of space cannot be apprehended, even so, Kauśika, the measure of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cannot be apprehended.

Due to the immeasurability of space, there is the immeasurability of conditioned phenomena; due to the immeasurability of conditioned phenomena, there is the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Kauśika, because consciousness is immeasurable, this perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is immeasurable. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no measure of consciousness is apprehended;
just as, Kauśika, no measure of space is apprehended.
In the same way, Kauśika, no measure of consciousness is apprehended;

because space is immeasurable, consciousness is immeasurable, and because consciousness is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable. Because the eye is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is immeasurable. For what reason?
For in this way, Kauśika, the measure of the eye is not apprehended; just as, Kauśika, the measure of space is not apprehended,
even so, Kauśika, the measure of the eye is not apprehended.
Because space is immeasurable, the eye is immeasurable; because the eye is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Because the ear is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is immeasurable. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no measure of the ear is apprehended.
Just as, Kauśika, the measure of space cannot be apprehended,
even so, Kauśika, the measure of the ear cannot be apprehended;
through the immeasurability of space, there is the immeasurability of the ear, and through the immeasurability of the ear, there is the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom.
Kauśika, because the nose is immeasurable, this perfection is immeasurable for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no measure of the nose is apprehended; just as, Kauśika, no measure of space is apprehended.
In the same way, Kauśika, no measure of the nose is apprehended;

because space is immeasurable, the nose is immeasurable, and because the nose is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable. Because the tongue is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is immeasurable. For what reason?
For in this way, Kauśika, no measure of the nose is apprehended;
just as, Kauśika, no measure of space is apprehended, even so, Kauśika, [no measure] of the tongue is apprehended.
No measure is perceived;
because space is immeasurable, the tongue is immeasurable, and because the tongue is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Because the body is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is immeasurable. For what reason?
For in this way, Kauśika, no measure of the body is apprehended; just as, Kauśika, no measure of space is apprehended,
even so, Kauśika, no measure of the body is apprehended.
Through the immeasurability of space, there is the immeasurability of the body; through the immeasurability of the body, there is the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom.
Because the mind is immeasurable, Kauśika, this perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is immeasurable. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, no measure of the mind is apprehended.
